name: Holiday Horror 3

date.source: The fed's own multi-part New Year's supercard posting, its own broadcast referring to New Year's decorations; the surviving posts carry only a capture timestamp rather than a confirmed thread date, so the exact day is not fixed.

evidence.source: The fed's own multi-part New Year's supercard posting, now served in full.
evidence.note: A three-city supercard (Tokyo, Tampa, Athens) closing with a sale of the promotion on-screen and a change of president.

matches.stipulation: Fifteen-man international battle royal for the newly introduced Cruiserweight Championship
matches.note: Introduced the title with a fifteen-man field; only the outgoing and incoming champions are structured here, and the winning elimination came with help from a masked ally at ringside. A further thirteen entrants are not named here.

matches.stipulation: Four-way Television Championship match with the rules changing every five minutes ("Choose Your Poison")
matches.note: The defending champion was blindfolded by his own ally's plan gone wrong and counted out by mistake. A fourth entrant in the match is not named here.

An impromptu American Championship defense, arranged on-air after the scheduled challenger missed his flight; the champion accepted the fed's own hardcore stipulation from an earlier match as the terms. The referee's final three-count was unusually fast.

The Ultimate Championship main event, decided by disqualification after New Alliance interference. The fed's new majority owner overruled the finish on-air rather than let a disqualification change the title, ordered a rematch, and handed the belt back to the defending champion at the show's close.

no_appearances_reason: The broadcast also carried a Colby Cup tournament, an Ultimate Death Match, tag team title action, and a lengthy undercard; only the four singles/battle-royal title matches above and the closing ownership angle are named here; the rest of the broadcast's own large supporting card is not.
notes: A three-city New Year's supercard (Tokyo, Tampa, Athens) on which all four of the fed's contested singles titles changed hands or were defended and a new Cruiserweight Championship was introduced. The broadcast closed with color commentator Magnus Colby revealing he had bought a controlling stake in the promotion; he fired sitting president Jay Steele and the head of security on-screen and installed a caretaker president through the fed's own next Ides of March pay-per-view.

name: The Ides of March '99

date.source: The fed's own multi-part pay-per-view posting; the surviving posts carry only a capture timestamp rather than a confirmed thread date, but the fed's own annual Ides of March pay-per-view fell on 15 March in both 1997 and 1998, and this edition is billed the same way.

evidence.source: The fed's own multi-part pay-per-view posting, now served in full.
evidence.note: A three-city pay-per-view (Mexico City, Tampa, Tokyo) built around a rematch the fed's own new ownership ordered at its prior show.

matches.note: American Championship defense; the challenger regained the title by pinfall in 22 minutes and 34 seconds.

The champion retained after a third challenger's own manager helped turn the finish; that third challenger is not named here. Kyle Kamikaze allowed himself to be counted out early in the match without explanation.
The defending champion retained on a guest referee's count that the broadcast itself called highly debatable; a post-match brawl drew in wrestlers from three different stables.

appearances.source: Served as the guest referee for the Ultimate Championship main event.

no_appearances_reason: The pay-per-view also carried a tag team tournament, a cruiserweight-adjacent tag match, and a lengthy supporting card across its three broadcast cities; only the three singles title matches above are named here; the rest of the broadcast's own large supporting card is not.
notes: The fed's own third consecutive Ides of March pay-per-view, broadcasting from Mexico City, Tampa and Tokyo. The Ultimate Championship rematch the fed's new ownership had ordered at its prior show is itself unattested in the surviving record; by this show the challenger from that earlier match has become champion himself, and the prior champion appears only as a guest commentator.
